questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 31-year-old male newly diagnosed with HIV infection returns to the clinic for his initial laboratory review. His baseline CD4 T-lymphocyte count is reported as 180 cells/μL. In addition to initiating combination antiretroviral therapy (ART), primary prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) should be immediately started using which threshold standard?

options.A: When the CD4 count drops below 500 cells/μL
options.B: When the CD4 count drops below 350 cells/μL
options.C: When the CD4 count drops below 200 cells/μL
options.D: When the CD4 count drops below 100 cells/μL

questions.explanation: Primary prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) using Co-trimoxazole (TMP-SMX) is strictly indicated in HIV-infected patients when their CD4+ T-cell count drops below 200 cells/μL (or if they develop an AIDS-defining illness like oral thrush). Prophylaxis for MAC is initiated below 50 cells/μL.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: An epidemiologist is reviewing malaria transmission dynamics in a specific zone. Among the non-falciparum human malaria species, which pathogen is uniquely characterized by having the longest incubation period (often ranging from 18 to 40 days) and a distinct propensity to cause immune complex-mediated nephrotic syndrome?
questions.explanation: Plasmodium malariae is responsible for quartan malaria (72-hour fever cycles) and possesses the longest incubation period among the common Plasmodium species. Chronic infection with P. malariae is uniquely linked to the development of immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis and nephrotic syndrome in children. Unlike P. vivax and P. ovale, it lacks a hypnozoite liver stage.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 38-year-old male with an unknown HIV status presents with a 3-week history of exertional dyspnea, non-productive cough, and low-grade fever. On examination, he is tachypneic and has oral candidiasis. Chest X-ray reveals diffuse, bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates, and arterial blood gas shows a PaO2 of 64 mmHg. Induced sputum stain confirms the presence of Pneumocystis jirovecii. Which of the following is the definitive first-line pharmacological treatment?

options.A: Fluconazole induction followed by oral itraconazole
options.B: High-dose Co-trimoxazole (Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole) combined with adjunctive corticosteroids

questions.explanation: The first-line therapeutic regimen for active Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is high-dose Co-trimoxazole (TMP-SMX) for 21 days. Because this patient's arterial blood gas demonstrates moderate-to-severe hypoxemia (defined as PaO2 < 70 mmHg or an alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient ≥ 35 mmHg), adjunctive corticosteroids must be co-administered before or with the first dose of antibiotics to prevent clinical deterioration driven by organism lysis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 26-year-old female is admitted during a monsoon outbreak with acute-onset high fever, severe retro-orbital headache, diffuse maculopapular rash, and profound myalgias. Laboratory testing confirms Dengue fever via NS1 antigen positive status. Her platelet count is noted to drop precipitously from 150,000/mm³ to 32,000/mm³ on day 4 of the illness. What is the primary underlying pathophysiology responsible for this severe thrombocytopenia?

options.A: Direct viral-induced bone marrow suppression exclusively
options.B: A combination of direct bone marrow suppression and antibody-mediated peripheral platelet destruction
options.C: Consumptive coagulopathy driven by low-grade disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
options.D: Splenic sequestration caused by acute portal hypertension

questions.explanation: Thrombocytopenia in Dengue virus infection is multifactorial. During the early phase, the virus causes direct acute bone marrow suppression, affecting megakaryocytopoiesis. In the later/critical phase, immune-mediated mechanisms dominate, where anti-dengue antibodies cross-react with platelets and endothelial cells, leading to accelerated peripheral platelet destruction and clearance.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: During an urban vector-borne disease outbreak, multiple patients present with acute febrile illnesses accompanied by skin rashes and musculoskeletal symptoms. When clinically differentiating Chikungunya virus infection from Dengue virus infection, which of the following features serves as the most prominent hallmark of Chikungunya?

options.A: Saddleback fever patterns that resolve within 48 hours
options.B: Severe, bilateral, and symmetrical polyarthralgias that can persist for months
options.C: A higher incidence of plasma leakage and hemorrhagic manifestations

questions.explanation: While both Dengue and Chikungunya present with fever, rash, and body aches, Chikungunya is classically distinguished by severe, debilitating, bilateral, and symmetrical polyarthralgias/arthritis targeting small joints of the hands and feet, which frequently progresses to a chronic phase lasting months or years. Dengue features more prominent retro-orbital pain, visceral plasma leakage, and profound cytopenias.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old male presents with a 2-week history of step-ladder fever, dry cough, abdominal pain, and constipation. On examination, bradycardia relative to the high fever is noted, along with faint erythematous macules on his abdomen. Which diagnostic test provides the highest diagnostic yield during the first week of this illness?
questions.explanation: The clinical picture of a step-ladder fever, relative bradycardia (Faget's sign), and rose spots on the abdomen points to Typhoid fever (Enteric fever caused by Salmonella typhi). During the first week of infection, blood cultures are the gold standard and have the highest diagnostic yield (approx. 90%), while stool cultures become positive later in weeks 2 and 3.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 29-year-old male presents with a painless, indurated ulcer with clean margins on his glans penis. Accompanied by painless bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy, primary syphilis is suspected. Which diagnostic investigation is preferred to directly visualize the organism from the ulcer exudate?
questions.explanation: A classic painless chancre indicates primary syphilis. Darkfield microscopy of serous fluid from the lesion provides immediate confirmation by visualizing the motile spirochetes (Treponema pallidum). Serological tests like VDRL and FTA-ABS can often yield false-negative results during the very early stages of a primary chancre.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 42-year-old sewage treatment worker presents with sudden high fever, severe myalgias (specifically tracking the calves), conjunctival suffusion without purulent discharge, and mild jaundice. Serum creatinine and bilirubin are elevated. Which pathogen is the most likely driver of this presentation?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of severe calf tenderness, conjunctival suffusion, occupational exposure to sewage or rodent urine, and renal/hepatic dysfunction characterizes severe Leptospirosis (Weil's disease), caused by the spirochete Leptospira interrogans.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old male with poorly controlled HIV (CD4 count 45 cells/μL) presents with a progressive headache, low-grade fever, and confusion over 3 weeks. Physical examination shows mild nuchal rigidity. Lumbar puncture reveals elevated opening pressure, low glucose, and high protein. Lumbar CSF stained with India ink reveals encapsulated yeast cells. What is the most appropriate induction therapeutic regimen for this patient?

options.A: High-dose oral fluconazole monotherapy for 8 weeks
options.B: Intravenous Liposomal Amphotericin B combined with Flucytosine for at least 2 weeks

questions.explanation: The patient has Cryptococcal meningitis, confirmed by India ink staining of CSF in an advanced immunosuppressed state. The guidelines call for an aggressive induction therapy consisting of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B plus oral flucytosine for a minimum of 2 weeks, followed by consolidation therapy with oral fluconazole.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 38-year-old HIV-positive patient (CD4 count 80 cells/μL) presents with focal neurological deficits, a high-grade fever, and generalized seizures. A contrast-enhanced brain MRI displays multiple ring-enhancing lesions localized within the basal ganglia with surrounding vasogenic edema. Brain biopsy reveals crescent-shaped tachyzoites. What is the standard drug regimen of choice for treating this infection?

options.A: Sulfadiazine and Pyrimethamine, supplemented with Leucovorin (folinic acid)
options.D: Pyrimethamine and Clindamycin without folinic acid

questions.explanation: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia of an AIDS patient are highly characteristic of Toxoplasma encephalitis, driven by Toxoplasma gondii. The preferred first-line therapeutic management consists of Pyrimethamine and Sulfadiazine. Leucovorin (folinic acid) must be co-administered to prevent bone marrow toxicity induced by pyrimethamine's antifolate mechanism.
